To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the classical capacitor and the inductor compensators are interpreted as energy equalizers, that PF improvement under nonsinusoidal supply voltage is equivalent to the existence of a compensator that imposes cyclodissipative behavior on the load, that the supply rate of the compensator is now function of its parameters instead of the load, and that the compensator that optimally improves the PF is not the one that equalizes the powers of inductances and capacitances of the load.

the PF of a nonlinear load can be improved by imposing cyclodissipative properties on its supply terminals, and that this is equivalent to imposing a condition of energy equalization between the supply and the compensator.

(1) a general condition for power factor improvement is that a certain equalization of the weighted powers of the inductors and the capacitors of a general linear compensator be achieved; and (2) the ideal power factor compensator is the one that minimizes the difference between the weighted powers.

the PF is the ratio between the real and apparent powers, where the apparent power is defined by the product of the rms voltage and rms current.
we provide a framework that allows us to characterize PF improvement for nonlinear loads in terms of energy flows, and to formulate the problem of PF improvement as an optimization problem.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the classical PF improvement compensators are not the optimal ones, and that there exists an optimal compensator, which is not a capacitor or inductor, but a general linear lossless circuit.
the PF improvement of nonlinear loads under non-sinusoidal conditions is equivalent to the property of cyclidissipativity of the load terminals.

PF improvement for nonlinear loads under nonsinsoidal conditions is equivalent to the imposition of a property of equalization of the weighted powers of the capacitive and inductive elements of the load.
